citations.quote: For $n=2$ or $3$, let $X=\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$ and let $X^{an}$ be its complex analytic space. Define analytification by $\mathcal F^{an}=\mathcal F\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}\mathcal O_{X^{an}}$. It is an exact tensor-compatible equivalence from algebraic coherent sheaves (locally finitely presented $\mathcal O_X$-modules) to holomorphic coherent sheaves. It identifies algebraic and holomorphic morphisms, preserves cohomology and the derived morphism groups $\operatorname{Ext}^q$, and commutes with restriction to the fixed hyperplane $L_\infty=\{z_0=0\}$. For an algebraic coherent sheaf $\mathcal E$ flat over a finite-type complex parameter scheme $S$, let $p:X\times S\to S$ be projection. Analytification commutes with the algebraic family structure and fiber restrictions. Whenever the algebraic and analytic higher direct images $R^qp_*\mathcal E$ are locally free and the natural maps from their residue-field fibers to $H^q(X_s,\mathcal E_s)$ are isomorphisms, the comparison identifies those direct images and base-change maps. No assertion is made that an arbitrary holomorphic family over a nonproper algebraic base algebraizes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) inherited from the finite
coherent-resolution and cohomological suppliers. A section $s$ of a rank-$d$
bundle $Q$ is a **regular section** here if, at each point of its zero scheme
$Z(s)$, some local frame expresses $s$ by $d$ components forming a regular
sequence of length $d$ in the local ring. Under this hypothesis it has exact
Koszul resolution
$\bigwedge^dQ^\vee\to\cdots\to Q^\vee\to\mathcal O\to\mathcal O_{Z(s)}\to0$.
Tensoring with a vector bundle preserves it. If a coherent sheaf $H$ has a
finite locally free resolution on a scheme and $t$ is a Cartier equation acting
injectively on $H$, restricting the resolution to $t=0$ remains exact and
resolves $H/tH$. In the deformation blowup for a closed embedding of smooth
quasi-projective varieties $i:X\hookrightarrow Y$, let $E$ be a finite
locally free sheaf on $X$. The strict transform
$F:X\times\mathbb P^1\hookrightarrow M$ is disjoint from
$B=\operatorname{Bl}_XY$, and a resolution of $F_*\operatorname{pr}_X^*E$
restricts exactly to the ordinary $Y$ fibre and to
$P=\mathbb P_{\mathrm{lines}}(N\oplus1)$; on $B$ it is an exact complex.

For an additive left-exact functor $F$ and a bounded-below complex $K$ with supplied Cartan–Eilenberg resolution $I$, there is a spectral sequence
$$E_1^{p,q}=R^qF(K^p)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathbb R_I^{p+q}F(K),\qquad d_r:(p,q)\mapsto(p+r,q-r+1).$$
Here $q\ge0$ and $p\ge b$ if $K^p=0$ for $p<b$. It is first quadrant after translating $p$ by $b$ and converges strongly with a finite filtration on every target degree. Derived objects use the supplied columns; under DC, or supplied Cartan–Eilenberg comparison and homotopy data, it is natural in $K$ and independent of the resolution from $E_1$ onward.

For an additive left-exact $F$ and bounded-below $K$ with supplied Cartan–Eilenberg resolution $I$, there is a strongly convergent spectral sequence
$$E_2^{p,q}=R^pF(H^qK)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathbb R_I^{p+q}F(K),\qquad d_r:(p,q)\mapsto(p+r,q-r+1).$$
Its support is $p\ge0,q\ge b$ for a lower bound $b$ of $K$; translate $q$ by $b$ to obtain a first quadrant. The target has a finite decreasing filtration by resolution degree. With DC or supplied Cartan–Eilenberg comparisons and homotopies, the sequence is natural and independent of the resolution from $E_2$ onward.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field and $n\ge0$, let
$X=\mathbb P^n_k$ with dualizing line bundle $\omega_X=\mathcal O(-n-1)$ and
residue trace $t_X:H^n(X,\omega_X)\to k$
([[def-smooth-projective-dualizing-line-bundle-and-trace]]), and let
$\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\mathcal O_X}$ be the global sheaf Ext of
[[def-sheaf-ext-for-coherent-modules]].

1. **(The pairing.)** For every coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module $F$, every
   $q\in\{0,\dots,n\}$, $\alpha\in\operatorname{Ext}^{n-q}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)$
   and $\eta\in H^q(X,F)$ set
   $$\langle\alpha,\eta\rangle_F\;:=\;t_X\Bigl(\chi^n_{\omega_X}\bigl(\alpha\cdot\chi^q_F{}^{-1}(\eta)\bigr)\Bigr),$$
   where $\chi^q_F:\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal O_X,F)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^q(X,F)$
   is the canonical isomorphism of
   [[lem-injective-modules-flasque-and-ext-of-structure-sheaf]],
   $\chi^q_F{}^{-1}(\eta)$ is the corresponding class in
   $\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal O_X,F)$, and
   $\alpha\cdot\beta\in\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal O_X,\omega_X)$
   is the Yoneda product of
   $\alpha\in\operatorname{Ext}^{n-q}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)$ with
   $\beta=\chi^q_F{}^{-1}(\eta)$, i.e. composition
   $\alpha\circ\beta$ of derived morphisms under
   $\operatorname{Ext}^{\bullet}_{\mathcal O_X}(-,-)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X))}(-,-[\bullet])$
   ([[thm-ext-is-hom-in-the-derived-category]],
   [[prop-yoneda-product-is-composition-in-the-derived-category]]). This
   **Serre duality pairing** is $k$-bilinear and natural in $F$.

2. **(Perfectness.)** For every coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module $F$ and every
   $q\in\{0,\dots,n\}$ the pairing
   $$\langle-,-\rangle_F:\operatorname{Ext}^{n-q}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)\times H^q(X,F)\longrightarrow k$$
   is a perfect pairing of $k$-vector spaces, i.e. both adjoint maps
   $\operatorname{Ext}^{n-q}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)\to H^q(X,F)^\vee$ and
   $H^q(X,F)\to\operatorname{Ext}^{n-q}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)^\vee$ are
   isomorphisms.

The case $q=n$ of clause 2 is the classical statement that
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)\to H^n(X,F)^\vee$,
$\varphi\mapsto(\eta\mapsto t_X(H^n(\varphi)(\eta)))$, is an isomorphism, and
for $F=\mathcal O_X$ clause 2 recovers $H^{n-q}(X,\omega_X)\cong H^q(X,\mathcal O_X)^\vee$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a commutative
ring with $1$ ([[def-commutative-ring]]), let $n\ge0$, let $d\in\mathbb Z$ and
let $X=\mathbb P^n_A\cong\operatorname{Proj}A[x_0,\dots,x_n]$ be relative
projective space ([[def-relative-projective-space-standard-charts]],
[[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]), with twisting sheaf
$\mathcal O_X(d)$ ([[def-twisting-sheaf-proj]]) and cohomology
$H^q(X,\mathcal O_X(d))$. Then
$$H^q(X,\mathcal O_X(d))=0\qquad\text{unless }q=0\text{ or }q=n.$$
If $n>0$, then $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))\cong A[x_0,\dots,x_n]_d$ when $d\ge0$
and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))=0$ when $d<0$, where
$A[x_0,\dots,x_n]_d$ is the degree-$d$ graded piece
([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]]); and $H^n(X,\mathcal O_X(d))$ is the
free $A$-module on the Laurent monomials $x_0^{e_0}\cdots x_n^{e_n}$ with
$e_i<0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_ie_i=d$, so that it is nonzero precisely when
$d\le-n-1$ and $A\ne0$. For $n=0$ one has $\mathbb P^0_A=\operatorname{Spec}A$
and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))\cong A$ for every $d\in\mathbb Z$, with all higher
groups zero. The zero ring $A=0$ is allowed: then $X=\varnothing$ and all
groups are zero, in agreement with both displayed descriptions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field and $n\ge0$, let
$S=k[x_0,\dots,x_n]$ be graded by total degree with $\deg x_i=1$, let
$\mathbb P^n_k=\operatorname{Proj}S$ with twisting sheaves
$\mathcal O(d)=\widetilde{S(d)}$, and let $F$ be a coherent
$\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n_k}$-module. Then there is a finitely generated graded
$S$-module $M$ with $\widetilde M\cong F$ and an exact sequence of graded
$S$-modules with degree-preserving maps
$$0\longrightarrow F_{n+1}\longrightarrow F_n\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow F_0\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow 0$$
in which every $F_i$ is a finite direct sum of shifted free modules $S(d)$
with $d\in\mathbb Z$, and whose sheafification
$$0\longrightarrow\widetilde F_{n+1}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow\widetilde F_0\longrightarrow F\longrightarrow 0$$
is an exact sequence of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n_k}$-modules in which every
$\widetilde F_i$ is a finite direct sum $\bigoplus_j\mathcal O(d_{ij})$ of
twisting sheaves. The resolution has length at most $n+1$: the displayed free
terms $F_0,\dots,F_{n+1}$ are finite direct sums of shifted free modules, any
of them may be zero, a shorter resolution is allowed when it terminates
earlier, and the truncation degree of $M$ is chosen so that $M$ is finitely
generated and $\widetilde M\cong F$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) inherited from the finite
coherent-resolution and cohomological suppliers. Let $Y$ be smooth
quasi-projective over a field and $E$ a rank-$r$ bundle. For
$q:P=\mathbb P_{\mathrm{lines}}(E)\to Y$, $K^0(P)=G_0(P)$ is generated as a
$K^0(Y)$-module by $\mathcal O(a)$, $0\le a<r$. For $r\ge1$ and $a\ge0$,
$q_!\mathcal O(a)=\operatorname{Sym}^a(E^\vee)$. For $r=0$, the projective
bundle is empty, its $K$-groups and all $q_!\mathcal O(a)$ are zero, and the
assertion of generation is vacuous. This statement has the
corresponding dual form for quotient projective bundles.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R\to S$ be a local homomorphism of
Noetherian local rings, let $I\subsetneq R$ be an ideal, and let $M$ be a
finite $S$-module. If $M/IM$ is flat over $R/I$ and the multiplication map
$$I\otimes_R M\longrightarrow M$$
is injective, then $M$ is flat over $R$. There is **no** assumption that
$M$ is finitely generated as an $R$-module.
Every finitely generated torsion-free module over a principal ideal domain is finite free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $I \trianglelefteq R$ satisfy $I \subseteq J(R)$, and let $M$ be a finitely generated left $R$-module. If $IM=M$, then $M=0$.

Assume AC and DC. On a regular Noetherian surface a coherent reflexive module is locally free. For a finite module $M$ over a normal Noetherian domain, a generic vector belonging to $M^{**}$ at every height-one localization belongs to $M^{**}$. For a coherent generic-rank-$r$ module on a regular surface, $(\wedge^rM)^{**}$ is the determinant line of $M^{**}$.

derivations.claim: Near a point of $L_\infty$, let $R$ be the regular local surface ring, $t$ a local equation of $L_\infty$, and $M$ the torsion-free stalk of $\mathcal E$. Multiplication by $t$ is injective on $M$. Lift a basis of $M/tM\cong(R/(t))^N$ to obtain a surjection $R^N\twoheadrightarrow M$ by Nakayama [F8]. If $K$ is its kernel, tensoring with $R/(t)$ is exact on the left because $t$ is injective on $M$; the lifted basis makes $(R/(t))^N\to M/tM$ an isomorphism, so $K/tK=0$. Nakayama [F8] gives $K=0$, proving local freeness of rank $N$ near the framed line.

Let $Q$ be the universal rank-two quotient bundle on the first factor. The section of $\mathcal O(1)$ on the second factor tensored with $Q$ on the first, induced by the second tautological line modulo the first, vanishes exactly on the diagonal. In affine coordinates transverse to the diagonal its two components are a regular parameter pair; hence its Koszul complex is exact and resolves $\mathcal O_\Delta$. Since $\det Q=\mathcal O(1)$ and $Q^*=\Omega^1(1)$, the resolution is $0\to\mathcal O(-1)\boxtimes\mathcal O(-2)\to\Omega^1(1)\boxtimes\mathcal O(-1)\to\mathcal O\boxtimes\mathcal O\to\mathcal O_\Delta\to0$. The regularity check is local along the diagonal, and outside it one component is a unit; this verifies exactness at every point. Its alternating $K$-class is the diagonal generator from [F5], but here the actual Koszul complex, rather than only its $K$-class, supplies the resolution.

The framing makes $\det\mathcal E$ trivial on $L_\infty$, so $c_1(\mathcal E)\cdot L_\infty=0$ and $\mu(\mathcal E)=0$. For a positive-rank subsheaf $\mathcal F\subset\mathcal E$, replace it by its saturation. At the generic point of $L_\infty$, use the chart $z_1\ne0$ with coordinates $x=z_0/z_1$, $y=z_2/z_1$; the local ring is $\mathbb C[x,y]_{(x)}$, a discrete valuation ring because every nonzero polynomial is a power of $x$ times a polynomial not divisible by $x$, and the latter is a unit after localization. Saturation makes both $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal E/\mathcal F$ torsion-free there, hence free by [F7]. Thus reducing the inclusion modulo $x$ remains injective at that generic point. Taking the double dual of its top exterior power gives a morphism from the determinant line of $\mathcal F$ to the corresponding exterior power of $\mathcal E$ near the line; [F9] makes this extension a morphism across the finite non-locally-free set. It is nonzero at the generic point and therefore restricts to a nonzero map $\det(\mathcal F)|_{L_\infty}\to\bigwedge^{\mathrm{rk}\mathcal F}(W\otimes\mathcal O_{L_\infty})$. Some component into a trivial line bundle is a nonzero section of $(\det(\mathcal F)|_{L_\infty})^*$, forcing $\deg(\det(\mathcal F)|_{L_\infty})\le0$. This proves slope-semistability of $\mathcal E$ of slope zero.

A nonzero section of $\mathcal E(-d)$ for $d=1,2$ would give a rank-one subsheaf of $\mathcal E$ whose determinant has degree at least $d>0$, contrary to step 2.1. Hence $H^0(\mathcal E(-1))=H^0(\mathcal E(-2))=0$. A nonzero map $\mathcal E\to\mathcal O(-d)$ for $d=1,2$ would have a torsion-free image that is a quotient of $\mathcal E$ of slope at least zero: its kernel is a subsheaf of the slope-zero semistable sheaf, so has degree at most zero, while $\deg\mathcal E=0$. The same image is a subsheaf of $\mathcal O(-d)$ of degree at most $-d$. This is impossible. By coherent Serre duality [F4], these Hom vanishings give $H^2(\mathcal E(-1))=H^2(\mathcal E(-2))=0$.

The Hilbert polynomial gives $\chi(\mathcal E(-1))=\chi(\mathcal E(-2))=-k$. With the vanishings of step 3.1, $h^1(\mathcal E(-1))=h^1(\mathcal E(-2))=k$. The Euler sequence is locally split, so tensoring it by $\mathcal E$ remains exact; its first map therefore injects $H^0(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)$ into $H^0(\mathcal E(-1))^3$, which is zero by step 3.1.

Serre duality identifies $H^2(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)^*$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal E,T_{\mathbb P^2}(-3))$. The twisted Euler sequence is $0\to\mathcal O(-3-d)\to\mathcal O(-2-d)^3\to T_{\mathbb P^2}(-3-d)\to0$. For $d\ge-1$, both $H^0$ terms on the left vanish and $H^1(\mathcal O(-3-d))=0$ by [F5], hence $H^0(T_{\mathbb P^2}(-3-d))=0$. Any rank-one torsion-free subsheaf of $T_{\mathbb P^2}(-3)$ of degree at least $-1$ would extend by double dual to a nonzero map $\mathcal O(d)\to T_{\mathbb P^2}(-3)$ for some $d\ge-1$, a contradiction. Thus $T_{\mathbb P^2}(-3)$ is stable of slope $-3/2$. A nonzero map from the slope-zero semistable $\mathcal E$ to this stable sheaf would have image both a quotient of slope at least zero and a subsheaf of negative slope, impossible. Consequently $H^2(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)=0$. From the Euler sequence and the Hilbert polynomial, $\chi(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)=3\chi(\mathcal E(-1))-\chi(\mathcal E)=-(2k+N)$, so $h^1(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)=2k+N$.

Tensor this resolution on its first factor by $\mathcal E(-1)$ and take derived pushforward to the second factor. The standard finite affine cover computes coherent cohomology by Čech [F5]; choose a Cartan–Eilenberg resolution of the resulting bounded complex. DC, obtained from AC by [F3], supplies compatible resolution comparisons. Filtering this one total complex in the two orders gives the first and second spectral sequences [F3]; the identity comparison of the total complex identifies their abutment and canonical edge maps. Thus no arbitrary splitting is used. By steps 3.1 and 5.1, all rows except $q=1$ vanish. The surviving row is $H^1(\mathcal E(-2))\mathcal O(-2)\to H^1(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)\mathcal O(-1)\to H^1(\mathcal E(-1))\mathcal O$. Its only cohomology is $\mathcal E(-1)$ in the middle because the diagonal resolution transforms $\mathcal E(-1)$ to itself. Twisting by $\mathcal O(1)$ gives the displayed monad. The dimensions are exactly those from steps 4.1 and 5.1.

For a finite-type algebraic base $S$, tensor the relative diagonal Koszul resolution by the flat family and use the assumed base-change isomorphisms [A1]. The direct-image terms are vector bundles of ranks $k,2k+N,k$, and the finite filtered complex commutes with residue-field restriction. On every fiber, step 6.1 gives the monad. The right end map is surjective on every fiber, hence surjective by Nakayama [F8], and its kernel $K$ is locally free. Locally on $S$, write the remaining exact sequence as $0\to P^{-1}\to K\to\mathcal E\to0$, with $P^{-1}$ and $K$ flat over the base. Tensoring by any residue field $k(s)$ stays injective at the left because the fiber complex is a monad on the whole projective plane. Thus $\operatorname{Tor}_1^{\mathcal O_{S,s}}(k(s),\mathcal E)=0$, equivalently the maximal-ideal multiplication map is injective. Since $\mathcal E$ is finite over the local ring of $\mathbb P^2\times S$, [F6] proves flatness over $S$. The same base-change maps identify the relative middle cohomology with the given family. This is precisely the family range stated and does not assert base change outside it.

Fix integers $N\ge1$ and $k\ge0$ and standard Hermitian spaces $V=\mathbb C^k$, $W=\mathbb C^N$. A framed ADHM linear datum is $x=(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ with $B_i\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, $I:W\to V$ and $J:V\to W$. Define the complex and real polynomial expressions

$$\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=[B_1,B_2]+IJ,\qquad \mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J.$$

The datum is stable if the vectors $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$, with $m\ge0$, $i_j\in\{1,2\}$ and $w\in W$, span $V$. It is costable if there is no nonzero subspace of $V$ invariant under both $B_i$ and contained in $\ker J$. It is regular if it is stable and costable. The group $GL(V)$ acts by $g\cdot x=(gB_1g^{-1},gB_2g^{-1},gI,Jg^{-1})$. Its unitary subgroup is $U(V)$.

Write $X^s=\{x:\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=0,\ x\text{ stable}\}$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}=\{x\in X^s:x\text{ costable}\}$ and, for real $\zeta\ge0$, $X_\zeta^U=\{x\in X^s:\mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=\zeta I_V\}$. Denote the corresponding orbit sets by $X^s/GL(V)$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}/GL(V)$ and $X_\zeta^U/U(V)$, with quotient topologies when discussing their analytic spaces. A word frame consists of $k$ columns obtained by fixed words in $B_1,B_2$ applied to fixed standard basis vectors of $W$.

For $T_{\mathbb C}=(\mathbb C^*)^2\times(\mathbb C^*)^N$, write $t_1,t_2,e_1,\ldots,e_N$ for the coordinate characters and put $h=\operatorname{diag}(e_1^{-1},\ldots,e_N^{-1})$. Its action is $(t_1,t_2,h)\cdot x=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ)$. The compact torus is its subgroup on which all characters have modulus one. The framing representation thus has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha^{-1}$ and its dual has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha$.

These are finite-dimensional matrix definitions. They do not assert a real/complex quotient correspondence, a sheaf or ASD identification, or a noncompact pushforward. In particular, positive-FI stability and zero-FI regularity are distinct conditions; neither an endpoint identification nor an ordinary ASD interpretation follows from this definition.

Assume AC. Fix $N\ge1$, $k\ge0$, standard Hermitian $V=\mathbb C^k$, $W=\mathbb C^N$ and ADHM data $x=(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ with the complex equation $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$. derivations.claim: Since stability says $I\ne0$, $IJ=0$ forces $J=0$. The real equation is then $|I|^2=\zeta$, so $I$ lies on the circle of radius $\sqrt\zeta$. The $U(1)$ gauge action multiplies $I$ by its phase and leaves scalar $B_1,B_2$ unchanged. It is transitive on that circle with trivial stabilizer; hence the quotient is exactly the unconstrained pair $(B_1,B_2)\in\mathbb C^2$. By [F2], this is the positive-FI stable quotient.

At zero real level, $J=0$ still follows from $I\ne0$ and $IJ=0$, while the real equation becomes $|I|^2=0$. This contradicts $I\ne0$, so the stable zero-level locus is empty. In the positive chamber, $J=0$ makes all of $V$ a nonzero invariant subspace in $\ker J$; the data are not costable. By [F3], their framed sheaves are not locally free.

Let $P\to S^4$ be any smooth principal $U(1)$ bundle. Smooth local connection forms glue by a smooth partition of unity [F5]. Parallel transport from the center of each closed hemisphere along radial segments gives a smooth trivialization: each transported frame solves a linear smooth ODE, and [F5] supplies its smooth dependence on the endpoint. Their transition is a map $g:S^3\to U(1)$. Pulling back the universal cover $\mathbb R\to U(1)$ gives a covering of $S^3$; its connected component through a chosen point is a connected cover, hence is one-sheeted by [F4]. Thus $g$ lifts to $\theta:S^3\to\mathbb R$. Since the covering is a local diffeomorphism and $g$ is smooth, the lift is smooth. The homotopy $\theta_s=(1-s)\theta+s\theta(x_0)$ makes $g$ null-homotopic. Reparameterize this homotopy to be constant near its final parameter and use it on a collar of one hemisphere; this changes that trivialization so the transition is constant and the local frames glue to a global frame. Hence $P$ is trivial. In that frame write the real connection form as $a$ and its curvature as $f=da$, so $df=0$. Then $f\wedge f=d(a\wedge f)$, and Stokes [F6] gives $\int_{S^4}f\wedge f=0$. If it is ASD, $f=-*f$, so $f\wedge f=-f\wedge *f=-|f|^2d\mathrm{vol}$. The zero integral forces $f=0$, and the charge in the Statement is zero. Thus no smooth charge-one $U(1)$ ASD connection exists, and that empty ordinary sector cannot equal the positive-FI quotient $\mathbb C^2$.
